newsitem.title: GREECE: ALICO-EUROBANK WANTS CHANGE IN PENSION FUND MGMT.
newsitem.headline: ALICO-EUROBANK WANTS CHANGE IN PENSION FUND MGMT.

text.p: Alico-Eurobank Mutual Funds said current pension fund management practices are not professional despite the national economy ministry's recent legislation to free up 20 percent of pension fund assets.
The fund management company said that pension fund assets reached 3.9 trillion drachmas at end-1996 based on Bank of Greece statistics. Of this amount, 2.75 trillion were invested in T-bills.

"If a significant portion of these assets had been placed in fixed income mutual funds and longer maturity state debt paper, pensioners would have benefited by an extra 50 billion drachmas annually," Alico-Eurobank said.
"History shows that such placements outperform (T-bills) by 100-150 basis points on average."
Seeking change to the current status quo in pension fund management, it proposed setting up a pension fund supervisory body modelled after the capital market commission.
Its members could include representatives from the labour and social security ministries, pension funds and professional investment managers.
"Such a commission would monitor and evaluate the investment policy of pension funds based on a quarterly report they would be required to submit," it said.
Furthermore, the pension fund commission would also evaluate proposals made by mutual fund managers as regards the investment management of pension funds.
Mutual fund companies could, in turn, set up specialised funds for pension fund assets.
"Assets would have to be allocated to fixed income mutual funds, 75-90 percent, with the remainder in equity growth funds," it said.
The asset allocation practice abroad is 55-65 percent fixed income and 35-45 percent equity growth as the investment philosophy is more mature, it said.

Alico-Eurobank said its shareholder, American International Group, had successfully contributed to pension fund reform in Chile, Singapore, Hong-Kong and Australia. The same know-how could be put to use in Greece. --George Georgiopoulos, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
